strings.text: The Canterville Ghost

An old English manor, an American family that does not believe in ghosts and offers theirs oil for his chains, and Sir Simon de Canterville, who murdered his wife and has not slept for three hundred years. You are Virginia, fifteen: will you stand with your laughing family, or beside the old murderer who asks you, once, to go with him through the wall? What is pity for one who did evil worth — and who pays for it?
A laughing family, a very tired ghost — and a girl of fifteen who has to choose where she stands.

Two on vermilion!
The laws of Nature are not going to be suspended for the British aristocracy

Leave the open box by the library

She locked her paints in the chest of drawers, and put the key under her pillow
He takes my paints

For Ginny’s paints!

Virginia had twice raced old Lord Bilton on her pony round the park, and the young Duke fell in love with her on the spot — and stayed till the autumn
Shall we ride to the brook tomorrow?
Today
Reckless Rupert, or the Headless Earl. Midnight. The corner of the corridor. The twins

Come and watch. From behind the door
Tell the boys: “Don’t”
Sir Simon. It is Virginia. Don’t go round the corner tonight
Young lady. Ghosts do not change their routes
Somebody told him

The twins doubled up with laughter. Virginia laughed out loud — and clapped her hand over her mouth
He is old. Leave him alone
Ginny’s on the ghost’s side!

I know
At midnight, through the wall, came a shriek — and her brothers’ laughter
Ginny’s on the ghost’s side! “He’s o-old!”

Warned. Me. As one helps an old woman across a puddle
He took to his bed. The stain appeared no more
Shall we ride?
Let’s
Can’t sleep? Neither can I. Sit down
Papa. If a person did something very bad — long, long ago — may one pity him?
One may pity anyone, Ginny. Paying his debts — no
Is this about our old man? Ginny, he killed his wife. And the butler shot himself because of him — Mrs Umney told us
So it was you who told him
About him again
My nose is longer, I believe
It is like me. Let it stand here
Your feet are like ice. Off to bed
Go. I’ll sit up a while. I can’t sleep anyway

Autumn
Autumn came. Virginia was back from a ride with Cecil, her habit torn on a hedge, and ran up the back stairs so that her mother would not see. The door of the Tapestry Chamber stood ajar
I am Red Reuben, or the Strangled…
Ah — the one who warns ghosts. I did not ask you to
And you laughed. Behind the door. I heard
“He’s old.” Your brothers shouted it under my door. Old. Hm
I am so sorry for you. But my brothers are going back to Eton soon. And then, if you behave yourself, no one will annoy you
Behave myself? I must rattle my chains, and groan through keyholes, and walk about at night. It is my only reason for existing
It is no reason at all for existing. And you have been very wicked. Mrs Umney told us you killed your wife
My wife was very plain, never had my ruffs properly starched, and knew nothing about cookery
Why, there was a buck I had shot in Hogley Woods, a magnificent pricket — and do you know how she had it sent up to table?
However, it is no matter now, for it is all over. And I don’t think it was very nice of her brothers to starve me to death
Though I did kill her
“Starved? Are you hungry? I have a sandwich”
Starved? Are you hungry? I have a sandwich
Thank you. I never eat anything now. But you are kind. Much nicer than the rest of your horrid, rude, vulgar, dishonest family
You killed her. Nothing else matters
The cheap severity of abstract morality. Exactly like your horrid, rude, vulgar, dishonest family
It is you who are rude and vulgar! And as for dishonest — who stole the paints out of my box?
I left them for you myself — and you made her green!
There was no red left. The emerald — yes, a mistake
To furbish up that ridiculous stain!
Well, really, where was I to get it? It is a very difficult thing to get real blood nowadays
Your brothers fired peas at me. At my knees, madam
I have not slept for three hundred years. I am so tired
Then why don’t you go to sleep?
Far away beyond the pine-woods there is a little garden. There the grass grows long and deep, there are the great white stars of the hemlock flower, and the nightingale sings all night long…
You are not listening
You mean the Garden of Death
To lie in the soft brown earth, and listen to silence. To have no yesterday, and no tomorrow
You can open its doors for me. For Love is always with you, and Love is stronger than Death
Have you ever read the old prophecy on the library window?

Oh, often. “When a golden girl can win prayer from out the lips of sin, when the barren almond bears, and a little child gives away its tears, then shall all the house be still.” I don’t know what it means
Weep with me for my sins — I have no tears. Pray with me for my soul — I have no faith. It will be dark there, and wicked voices will whisper in your ear. They will not harm you
Ginny! Supper!
I shall not ask a second time
“I am not afraid. I will ask the Angel for you”
“No. I’ll call Papa”
I am not afraid. I will ask the Angel to have mercy on you
Ginny!
No. I’ll call Papa

You told us about him before. I believe you
How many times have you been to him, Ginny?
She did not answer. Her father touched her forehead — then looked at her a long while, and stopped smiling
Sir?
We are going to London. Tomorrow morning, all of us
And the ghost?
Virginia! Ginny!
Give her back!
The gypsies were camped by the field
Hoofbeats in the yard: Mr Otis and Cecil galloped off to the gypsy camp. Mrs Otis sat in the hall in her shawl, and did not get up
Promise me: never alone. Not to him, not after him
I promise
She took her hand back first. Her father held his out a moment longer
I’ll sit here. I can’t sleep anyway
You promised Papa: “Never alone.”
You said then: “You killed her. Nothing else matters.” Do you think so still?
For the first time in three hundred years Sir Simon walked down the corridor without a single sound
I have come to take my leave. It is the custom

Of everyone. Even of those who read me morals
I will come
You promised your father. I heard
She took half a step over the threshold, and stopped. He did not turn
Good night, Miss Virginia
Sir. My daughter stays
The clock struck, and with its last stroke the whole house fell silent
How could you!
Papa, I have been with the ghost. He is dead. Come
He said her name
He was a very wicked man. I prayed for him
The almond! The dry almond has blossomed!
The clock struck — and the whole house fell silent at once
Sir. Ginny
You promised
Yes
Show me
He did not give her his hand. She led him behind the tapestry, down a narrow passage in the wall, into the secret chamber
Go back, little Virginia! Go back!
Do not listen
Her hand lost his in the dark and searched — and his found hers by itself
Pray with me. I do not remember the words. Of her — we will not speak
She prayed aloud, and he repeated it after her, word for word
Lord, have mercy on him — and give rest to Lady Eleanore
Madam, I said: of her we will not speak. I am Sir Simon de Canterville, and I do not bargain at a graveside
Eleanore
There. Your father would be pleased: a bargain
He repeated the prayer to the end — for her, then for himself — and did not look at Virginia. The nightingale sang no more
Lord, let him sleep
And a little child gave away its tears: Virginia wept — for him
His hand slipped out of hers by itself
Farewell
Epilogue
Mr Otis had slept badly before. From that night until they left Canterville he did not sleep at all
Four days later, at night, they buried him in the churchyard under the old yew
We shall stay four more days. A funeral
Whose, Hiram?
Ask Virginia
His. I went with him in the night. I promised Papa — and I went
Ginny?
She said nothing; her father said nothing too. Her mother looked from one to the other
Leave it. It is his house. At a valuation
It has gone quiet. Quite quiet
That morning her candle-end lay at her door. She took it with her
I believe I fell asleep in the night. Forgive me, Ginny
She said nothing, and took his hand
Her father was beside her all morning, and never took his eyes off the windows of the Tapestry Chamber
The porch; the carriages.
Years later.
You have never told me what happened to you that night
Don’t ask me, Cecil. He showed me what Life is, and what Death signifies, and why Love is stronger than both
You may keep your secret, as long as I have your heart
You have always had it
And you will tell our children some day, won’t you?
The Otises kept Canterville, and came there every summer
I promise you, sir, she will write every week
Promise for yourself, Your Grace
They say that at Canterville they still rattle chains at night, and the new owners buy lubricant

The Candle
A quarter to midnight. A candle, and the long corridor to the Tapestry Chamber.
The flame is out. The corridor is dark to its end.
The Door
In the corridor: chains, steps, a groan. The door is shut.

Everyone is laughing. The window is dark, and the rain lashes it.

Darkness. Shapes, wings, whispers — and his pale hand.
Her hand has lost his. Hold on again — the dark is not over.

You kept the face in the window to yourself.

You watched with your brothers — and laughed out loud.

“You killed her. Nothing else matters.” He called it cheap morality.
You took his hand. Downstairs they were calling you to supper.

You prayed for him alone. Nobody said her name.
You walked past the chair. Your word to Papa is broken.
You stayed at the door. He went, and nobody but you knows.
You woke Papa. Sir Simon’s farewell was his: “My daughter stays.”
